title: If three instances of a service run and another service sends a Kafka message, how do you ensure only one instance consumes it (same consumer group)?
shortTitle: Ensuring only one of three service instances consumes a Kafka message

s1_definition.profdef: You ensure only one instance consumes each message by configuring all three instances with the same consumer group id. Within a single consumer group, Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer, so a given record — which lives in one partition — is delivered to only one instance of the group. The other instances in the same group will not receive that record. If instead each instance used a different group id, every instance would form its own group and all three would receive the same record, which is the opposite of what we want.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine three clerks at National Bank of India all employed on the same team to process incoming transfer slips. Because they are one team sharing one job, the supervisor hands each slip to only one clerk; the other two never see it. That is a single consumer group. If, by mistake, each clerk were treated as a separate one-person team, the supervisor would photocopy every slip and give a copy to all three, and the same transfer would be processed three times. Putting them in the same team — the same group id — is what guarantees single processing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Give all instances the same consumer group id so each message is processed by exactly one instance.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You ensure only one instance consumes each message by configuring all three instances with the same consumer group id. Within a single consumer group, Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer, so a given record — which lives in one partition — is delivered to only one instance of the group. The other instances in the same group will not receive that record. If instead each instance used a different group id, every instance would form its own group and all three would receive the same record, which is the opposite of what we want.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine three clerks at National Bank of India all employed on the same team to process incoming transfer slips. Because they are one team sharing one job, the supervisor hands each slip to only one clerk; the other two never see it. That is a single consumer group. If, by mistake, each clerk were treated as a separate one-person team, the supervisor would photocopy every slip and give a copy to all three, and the same transfer would be processed three times. Putting them in the same team — the same group id — is what guarantees single processing.

**One line to remember:** Give all instances the same consumer group id so each message is processed by exactly one instance.

sections.s2_technical:
The behavior hinges entirely on the group id. In Spring Boot you set it once with `spring.kafka.consumer.group-id=transfer-processor`, and you deploy three instances of the service, all reading this same property. Because they share the group id, Kafka's group coordinator treats them as one group and divides the topic's partitions among them. A record sits in exactly one partition, and that partition is owned by exactly one of the three instances, so only that instance receives and processes the record.

Concretely, suppose the topic `transfers` has three partitions and you run three instances with the same group id. Kafka assigns partition 0 to instance A, partition 1 to instance B, and partition 2 to instance C. When the producing service sends a transfer keyed by account id SAV2001, Kafka hashes the key to, say, partition 2, so only instance C consumes it. Instances A and B never see that message. This is the standard competing-consumers pattern built into Kafka.

A listener looks like this: `@KafkaListener(topics = "transfers", groupId = "transfer-processor") public void onTransfer(TransferEvent e) { ... }`. When this exact code runs in three instances with the same group id, Kafka guarantees that any single transfer event is handled by only one of them. The parallelism you gain is that three partitions are processed simultaneously by the three instances, so throughput roughly triples while each message is still processed once.

The common mistake is letting each instance generate a unique group id, for example by appending the hostname or a random suffix. That turns each instance into its own group, and since every group receives all partitions, all three instances would consume the same message, causing triple processing — three debits, three notifications. So the rule is simple: for competing consumers where each message is processed once, keep the group id identical across instances; for broadcast where every instance must see every message, give each instance a distinct group id.

There is an important edge case about partition count. If the topic has only one partition but you run three instances in the same group, only one instance will ever be active because a partition can be owned by just one consumer; the other two sit idle as hot standbys. They still provide failover — if the active instance dies, a rebalance hands the partition to one of the idle instances. To actually use all three instances in parallel, the topic needs at least three partitions.

For correctness under failure you also think about delivery semantics. Even within a single group, a rebalance after a crash can cause a message to be redelivered to a different instance if the offset was not committed before the crash, giving at-least-once delivery. So the consumer should be idempotent — for example checking whether a transfer id was already processed before applying it — so that a rare redelivery does not double-debit the account. The senior-level nuance is that same-group-id guarantees single consumption in the normal case, and idempotency guarantees single effect even across the rare redelivery during failover.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs three instances of its transfer-processing service behind a load balancer for availability, and a separate payments service sends transfer events to Kafka.

Problem 1 — When the payments service sends a transfer event for Rajesh, exactly one of the three instances must debit his account. If more than one processes it, Rajesh is debited multiple times. This is exactly the same-group-id requirement — all three instances share one group so only one gets the message.

Problem 2 — The team wants all three instances actually working at peak, not two sitting idle. This is exactly the partition-count requirement — the topic must have at least three partitions so each instance owns one and they process in parallel.

Problem 3 — If one instance crashes mid-processing, the transfer must not be lost or double-applied. This is exactly the idempotency requirement — the consumer checks a processed-transfer record so a redelivery after rebalance has no double effect.

The mini-project simulates three instances in one group. We build a `TransferEvent` domain object, a `Topic` with three partitions, a `TransferProcessor` representing one instance with idempotent handling via a shared processed-id set, and a `ConsumerGroupRuntime` that assigns partitions to instances and delivers each event to only its owning instance. The demo sends several transfers and shows each handled by exactly one instance, plus a redelivery that is safely ignored.

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml — the SAME group id on all three instances
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka1:9092,kafka2:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: transfer-processor   # identical on every instance => one group
      enable-auto-commit: false      # manual commit after processing (at-least-once)
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three transfer events TXF-1, TXF-2, TXF-3, plus a redelivery of TXF-1.

Step 1 — Three instances start, all with group id transfer-processor. Because the group id is identical, Kafka treats them as one group. The topic transfers has 3 partitions, so the runtime assigns partition 0 to instance-A, partition 1 to instance-B, partition 2 to instance-C. Each partition has exactly one owner.

Step 2 — The payments service sends TXF-1 keyed by SAV2001. Kafka hashes SAV2001 to a partition, say partition 2, which is owned by instance-C. Only instance-C receives TXF-1. It is new, so instance-C records the id and debits SAV2001. Instances A and B never see it.

Step 3 — TXF-2 keyed by CUR3001 hashes to a different partition, say partition 0, owned by instance-A. Only instance-A processes it. TXF-3 keyed by SAV9999 lands on partition 1, owned by instance-B. Now all three instances are working in parallel, each handling its own partition's messages.

Step 4 — A rebalance causes the payments flow to redeliver TXF-1. It again routes to partition 2 and instance-C. But instance-C checks the shared processed-id store, sees TXF-1 was already processed, and ignores it. Rajesh is debited only once despite the redelivery.

Step 5 — The logs show each transfer handled by exactly one instance, parallel processing across instances, and the duplicate safely ignored, proving that same-group-id plus idempotency gives single processing and single effect.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Payments service: send("transfers", key=accountId, TransferEvent)
    │
    ▼
  Topic transfers (3 partitions)   |   Group id = "transfer-processor" (ALL instances)
    │ partitionFor(key)
    ├─ P0 ─────────────→ instance-A  (owns P0)
    ├─ P1 ─────────────→ instance-B  (owns P1)
    └─ P2 ─────────────→ instance-C  (owns P2)

  TXF-1 (SAV2001) → P2 → ONLY instance-C processes → debit once
  TXF-2 (CUR3001) → P0 → ONLY instance-A
  TXF-3 (SAV9999) → P1 → ONLY instance-B

  Redeliver TXF-1 → P2 → instance-C → processedIds.contains → IGNORE

  WRONG setup (different group id per instance):
    each instance = its own group → ALL THREE receive TXF-1 → triple debit
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Single-Consumption via Group Id + Idempotency ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Competing Consumers: group splits partitions one owner each  │
  │    WHY: each message processed by exactly one instance       │
  │ Idempotent Receiver: processed-id guard                      │
  │    WHY: safe under redelivery during rebalance               │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Runtime assigns; Processor processes; Topic routes        │
  │ O: scale to more instances (up to partition count), no edits │
  │ D: Runtime depends on TransferProcessor abstraction          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │      ConsumerGroupRuntime      │
  │ - groupId: String             │
  │ - instances: List<Processor>  │ ◇ aggregation
  │ - owner: Map<partition,Proc>  │
  │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │ + assign(): void              │  one partition → one instance
  │ + deliver(key, event): void   │  routes to the single owner
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ delivers to
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │       TransferProcessor        │  (one running instance)
  │ - instanceId: String          │
  │ - processedIds: Set<String>   │ ◇ shared idempotency store
  │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │ + onTransfer(event): void     │  skip if already processed
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a transfer event ───────────────────────────

  [SENT] → routed to one partition → [OWNED by one instance]
        → new id? → [PROCESSED] (debit once)
        → duplicate id? → [IGNORED]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. group.assign()  → P0:A, P1:B, P2:C
  2. group.deliver("SAV2001", TXF-1) → P2 → instance-C.onTransfer()
  3.   → processedIds.add("TXF-1") true → debit SAV2001
  4. group.deliver("SAV2001", TXF-1) (redelivery) → instance-C.onTransfer()
  5.   → processedIds.add("TXF-1") false → IGNORE

  Contract for deliver(key, event):
    Pre:  group assigned
    Post: exactly one instance receives the event
    Guarantee: duplicate id has no second effect (idempotent)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To ensure only one of three service instances consumes a given Kafka message, I configure all three instances with the same consumer group id. Within a single consumer group, Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer, and since every record lives in exactly one partition, that record is delivered to only one instance. The other two instances in the group never receive it. In Spring Boot this is a single property, spring.kafka.consumer.group-id, set identically on every instance.

The classic mistake, which I always warn about, is letting each instance generate a unique group id, for example by appending the hostname. That turns each instance into its own group, and because every group receives all partitions, all three instances would process the same message, causing a triple debit. So the rule is: for competing consumers where each message is handled once, keep the group id identical; for broadcast where every instance must see every message, give each a distinct group id.

To actually use all three instances in parallel, the topic needs at least three partitions, so each instance owns one and they process simultaneously. If the topic had only one partition, only one instance would be active and the other two would sit idle as hot standbys, still useful for failover because a rebalance would hand the partition to a surviving instance if the active one died.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, three instances of the transfer processor share the group id transfer-processor, so any transfer event from the payments service is debited by exactly one instance. I pair this with idempotency — a unique constraint on the transfer id and a processed-id check — because a rebalance after a crash can redeliver a message with at-least-once semantics. The senior insight is that the same group id guarantees single consumption in the normal case, and idempotency guarantees a single effect even across the rare redelivery during failover, so Rajesh is never double-debited.
